title: Adab of eating
hook: a forgotten bismillah, said late, and the three table instructions taken one at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of speech, and your line: good, or silent. Did one reply wait a breath before it went out? Today the manners move from the tongue to the table. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

Three bites into dinner, a fork stops in midair. The bismillah. Forgotten. Too late now? A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud and Jami' al-Tirmidhi answers exactly that worry. Whoever forgets the name of Allah at the start, it says, should say it when they remember: in the name of Allah, at its beginning and its end. The name can arrive late and still cover the whole meal. Two days ago, a boy at the Prophet's table heard three short instructions. Today the path sits down with them, one at a time.
screen: `A FORK IN MIDAIR.` → `THE BISMILLAH, FORGOTTEN.` → `AT ITS BEGINNING AND ITS END.`

segments.voice: The three instructions come from 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah's report in Sahih al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: young man, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. Each one is small enough for a child. The first is bismillah, in the name of Allah. It turns a plate into a gift with a giver, and, as Abu Dawud's hadith says, it can come late. The second is the right hand, which hadith in Sahih Muslim ask for in eating and in drinking. The third is the one that's easy to miss: eat from what's near you. At a shared dish, the far side is in someone else's reach. It's courtesy turned into geography. You don't reach across your neighbor for the best piece. Then one more line about the table, from Abu Hurayrah, in Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, never criticized food. If he liked it, he ate it. If he didn't, he left it. No speech about it. That ties yesterday to today. The adab of eating includes the adab of speaking about what you eat. And the Qur'an frames the whole meal as a gift. In al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Eat of the good things wherewith We have provided you, and render thanks to Allah." Eat, and thank. The name, even late. The right hand. The near side. No complaints. None of it is elaborate. It's a meal anyone could eat this way tonight.
screen: `BISMILLAH: THE PLATE HAS A GIVER.` · `THE RIGHT HAND.` · `EAT FROM WHAT'S NEAR YOU.` · `NEVER A WORD AGAINST THE FOOD.`

segments.voice: The practice: eat one meal this way. For now, settle and breathe, and choose the meal: the next one you'll eat, at a table or at a desk. Walk through it slowly. The plate arrives. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah. If not, simply pause and notice where the food came from: the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. See your right hand reach for it. See yourself eating from your own side of the plate. And if something isn't to your taste, see yourself leaving it, quietly, without a word. The bell holds the time.
Adab of eating. The manners of the table: begin with the name of Allah, eat with the right hand, eat from what's near, and say nothing against the food. Today's word.

Your line: the right hand, the name. At your next meal, begin with a pause or a bismillah, and stay on your own side of the plate. Tomorrow, a third for food. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating, eat and drink with the right hand, and teach children to eat from the side of the dish nearest them, following the hadith of 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah.

fork.reveal: the name can arrive late: say it when you remember, at its beginning and its end.

what a scholar hears: a hadith told by 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, the Prophet's stepson, about his own childhood, and a remedy for the forgotten bismillah.
